verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Haridwar OEM-linked component and dealer borrowers with strong balance sheets; avoid small fleet operators and e-rickshaw financiers until local demand and enforcement settle.
title: Haridwar Cars & Commercial Vehicles (OEM): a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**Haridwar's auto cluster is OEM-linked component and assembly work plus a dealer and fleet layer that lives off vehicle sales and permits.** Inputs are steel, castings, plastics and power; output is parts and vehicles sold to OEMs or retail buyers. Cash sits in inventory and receivables, not in the plant. **So when a proposal lands, check the receivable days against the OEM's payment cycle and the inventory turn against the model cycle; if receivables stretch beyond the OEM's stated terms, ask for the buyer-wise ageing.**

## What has changed now
**The national picture is strong but the local picture is weak, and that gap is the whole story.** India-wide IIP for NIC 29 (motor vehicles) is +25.2% YoY and +19.2% Apr-to-date [D], and peers report healthy volumes: M&M automotive revenue +25% to ₹31,115 crore with EBIT margin 9.5% [5], Tata Motors CV volumes +26% with net profit ₹2,560 crore [6]. **But Uttarakhand GST collections are -19.1% Apr-to-date against India +6.1%, and electricity demand +4.7% against India +9.5% [D] — the state is running well behind the country.** Locally, the transport department seized 35 vehicles and issued 120 challans in Haridwar [1], and auto, vikram and e-rickshaw drivers protested the new electric bus and e-golf cart service [2][3]. **So when a fleet or passenger-transport proposal lands, check permit validity and challan history first; if the borrower's route overlaps the new electric bus corridor, ask how much of monthly collection comes from that route.**

## Where the growth is
**Pursue tier-2 component suppliers and authorised dealers tied to the OEMs that are actually growing, not the passenger-transport operators being displaced.** The peer results show volume-led growth at M&M and Tata Motors [5][6], and margin pressure from commodity and freight costs is the common thread [4][7]. **So when a component supplier lands, check whether the order book is with a growing OEM and whether price escalation clauses exist; if the contract is fixed-price with no commodity pass-through, ask for the last two quarters' gross margin.** Rating methodology for auto component suppliers and CV makers stresses cash-flow adequacy and leverage [10][11]; use those as the frame. **Avoid small e-rickshaw and vikram operators and single-route fleet owners until the permit dispute resolves.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the working-capital cycle, not the balance sheet.** Take monthly stock and debtor statements, a quarterly CMA, and a monthly challan and permit status for any transport borrower. **Take post-dated cheques or escrow of OEM receivables where the buyer is a large OEM; if the borrower resists, ask why the OEM payment cannot be routed.** Keep tenor within one model cycle. **Collect from customer the local order-book value and the OEM-wise sales split — the sources do not give Haridwar-specific auto output.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the local demand signals monthly, not the national ones.** A further fall in Uttarakhand GST or electricity demand [D], a rise in vehicle seizures [1], or widening protests against electric services [2][3] are the triggers. **If any two fire in the same month, freeze new transport-sector limits and review existing ones.**
watch: two consecutive months below India growth -> pause new transport limits
Vehicle seizure and challan reports in Haridwar (monthly)
rise in seizures -> recheck permits and challan history on all fleet borrowers
receivable days stretch beyond OEM terms -> ask for buyer-wise ageing and escrow
Electric bus and e-rickshaw protest news (monthly)
escalation on the new corridor -> cut exposure to affected route operators
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
